encounters.title: Layer 1: The Physical Foundation
encounters.scenario:
At the foundation of all networking is Layer 1, the Physical Layer. This layer deals with the actual transmission of raw bits as electrical signals, light pulses, or radio waves. It defines the physical media: copper cables (Cat5e, Cat6, Cat6a), fiber optic cables (SMF, MMF), and wireless radio frequencies.

Key concepts at this layer:
- Cabling standards and connector types (RJ45, LC, SC)
- Signal encoding (how 1s and 0s are represented electrically)
- Topology types (Bus, Star, Ring, Mesh)
- Bandwidth and throughput limitations
- Signal attenuation and interference

Devices operating here: Hubs, Repeaters, Cables, NICs (physical interface)

Without a functioning Physical Layer, no higher-layer communication can occur.
encounters.question: Which of the following operates at Layer 1 (Physical Layer)?
encounters.explanation: Hubs operate at Layer 1. They simply regenerate and forward electrical signals to all ports. Routers operate at Layer 3, switches primarily at Layer 2, and firewalls at Layers 3-7.

encounters.title: Layer 2: Data Link - MAC Addresses and Frames
encounters.scenario:
Layer 2, the Data Link Layer, provides node-to-node communication within the same local network. The key concept here is the MAC ADDRESS (Media Access Control) - a 48-bit hardware address burned into every network interface card (NIC).

Format: XX:XX:XX:XX:XX:XX (6 hexadecimal pairs)
- First 3 pairs: OUI (Organizationally Unique Identifier) - identifies the manufacturer
- Last 3 pairs: Device-specific identifier

Layer 2 organizes data into FRAMES. Each frame contains:
- Source MAC address
- Destination MAC address
- Type/Length field
- Data payload
- Error checking (CRC)

Switches operate at Layer 2, using a MAC address table (CAM table) to forward frames only to the correct port.
encounters.question: What is the purpose of a MAC address in networking?
options: Identify a device within a local network segment
encounters.explanation: MAC addresses uniquely identify devices within a local network segment (Layer 2). They are used for local delivery of frames, not global routing.

encounters.title: Layer 3: Network - IP Addressing and Routing
encounters.scenario:
Layer 3, the Network Layer, enables communication BETWEEN different networks. This is where IP (Internet Protocol) operates.

IPv4 addresses are 32-bit numbers, typically written in dotted decimal notation (e.g., 192.168.1.100). Each address has two parts:
- Network portion: Identifies which network the device is on
- Host portion: Identifies the specific device on that network

The subnet mask determines where the split occurs (e.g., 255.255.255.0 means first 3 octets are network, last is host).

ROUTERS operate at Layer 3. They:
- Examine destination IP addresses
- Look up routes in a routing table
- Forward packets toward their destination across network boundaries
- Connect different subnets and networks

Without Layer 3, networks would be isolated islands.
encounters.question: A packet needs to travel from Network A to Network B. Which device facilitates this at Layer 3?
encounters.explanation: Routers operate at Layer 3 and forward packets between different networks based on IP addresses.

encounters.title: Layer 4: Transport - TCP and UDP
encounters.scenario:
Layer 4, the Transport Layer, manages end-to-end communication between applications on different hosts. The two primary protocols are TCP and UDP.

TCP (Transmission Control Protocol):
- Connection-oriented (three-way handshake)
- Reliable delivery (acknowledgments, retransmissions)
- Flow control and congestion control
- Used for: Web browsing (HTTP), Email, File transfers

UDP (User Datagram Protocol):
- Connectionless (no handshake)
- Unreliable (best effort, no retransmissions)
- Low overhead, faster
- Used for: Video streaming, VoIP, DNS queries, online gaming

Port numbers identify specific applications/services:
- Port 80: HTTP
- Port 443: HTTPS
- Port 22: SSH
- Port 53: DNS
encounters.question: Which protocol should be used for a video conferencing application requiring real-time delivery with minimal latency?
encounters.explanation: UDP is preferred for real-time applications like video conferencing because it has lower latency. TCP's reliability mechanisms (retransmissions) would cause delays.

encounters.title: Layers 5-7: Session, Presentation, Application
encounters.scenario:
The top three layers work closely together and are often implemented by the same application.

Layer 5 - SESSION:
Manages connections/dialogues between applications. Establishes, maintains, and terminates sessions. Handles authentication and authorization during sessions.

Layer 6 - PRESENTATION:
Handles data formatting, encryption/decryption, and compression.
- SSL/TLS encryption happens here
- Data conversion (e.g., EBCDIC to ASCII)
- Image/audio format handling

Layer 7 - APPLICATION:
The interface users interact with. Protocols include:
- HTTP/HTTPS (web)
- FTP (file transfer)
- SMTP/POP3/IMAP (email)
- SSH (secure shell)

These layers are closest to the end user and furthest from the physical transmission.
encounters.question: At which layer does SSL/TLS encryption occur?
encounters.explanation: SSL/TLS encryption occurs at Layer 6 (Presentation Layer), which handles data formatting and security transformations.
